title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
tagline: Timeless lessons on wealth, greed and happiness: doing well with money is about behaviour.

superpower.name: Calm Investor
superpower.description: You stay reasonable when markets aren't.

overview: Housel argues that financial success depends less on intelligence than on behaviour, which is hard to teach. Through 20 short stories he covers luck and risk, compounding, saving, room for error and why reasonable often beats rational.

chapters.title: No One's Crazy
chapters.summary: People's money decisions reflect the era and experiences they lived through — inflation, crashes, booms. Behaviour that looks crazy to you can make sense from inside someone else's history. Your personal experience is a small slice of what's possible, yet it shapes your view of how the world works.
keyIdeas: What seems irrational may make sense to them.
Your view is a narrow sample.
chapters.tryThis: Ask an older relative what their worst money period taught them.

quiz.question: Why do people make different money decisions?
options: Different life experiences shape their views

chapters.title: Luck & Risk
chapters.summary: Luck and risk are two sides of the same coin: outcomes depend on forces beyond individual effort. Be careful whom you praise and whom you look down on, focus on broad patterns rather than individual cases, and remember that neither success nor failure is entirely earned.
keyIdeas: Luck and risk mirror each other.
chapters.tryThis: Write down one success of yours where luck played a part.

quiz.question: What does Housel say luck and risk are?
options: Two sides of the same coin
quiz.explanation: Both are forces beyond individual effort.

chapters.title: Never Enough
chapters.summary: Some wealthy people risk what they have and need for what they don't need. The hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving. Knowing when you have 'enough' protects you from ruinous risks and endless comparison.
keyIdeas: Don't risk what you need for what you don't.
chapters.tryThis: Write what 'enough' means for you in numbers.

quiz.question: What is the hardest financial skill per Housel?
options: Getting the goalpost to stop moving

chapters.title: Confounding Compounding
chapters.summary: Most of Warren Buffett's fortune came after his sixties, because he invested for decades. Compounding is counterintuitive: time is the most powerful factor. Good returns sustained over a long period beat spectacular returns that can't be kept up.
chapters.tryThis: Calculate what a monthly saving grows to over 30 years.

quiz.question: What's the biggest driver of Buffett's wealth according to Housel?
options: Investing for a very long time

chapters.title: Getting Wealthy vs. Staying Wealthy
chapters.summary: Getting money requires risk-taking and optimism; keeping it requires humility and fear that it can disappear. Survival — staying in the game long enough for compounding to work — matters most. Plan for plans not going to plan.
keyIdeas: Getting rich and staying rich need different skills.
chapters.tryThis: Identify one risk that could wipe you out and reduce it.

quiz.question: What matters most for staying wealthy?
quiz.explanation: Avoid ruin so compounding can work.

chapters.title: Tails, You Win
chapters.summary: A small number of events drive most outcomes. In investing, a few winners can account for most returns, so you can be wrong much of the time and still do well. Long tails mean persistence through many misses.
keyIdeas: A few events drive most results.
You can be wrong often and still win.
chapters.tryThis: Look at a portfolio or project and find the few items driving most results.

quiz.question: What does 'tails' refer to?
options: Rare events that drive most outcomes

chapters.title: Freedom
chapters.summary: The highest dividend money pays is the ability to control your time. Having control over what you do, when and with whom is a strong predictor of happiness — more than income alone.
chapters.tryThis: Estimate how many months of expenses you could cover without income.

quiz.question: What is money's highest dividend per Housel?

chapters.title: Man in the Car Paradox
chapters.summary: When people see someone in a fancy car, they rarely think 'that person is cool'; they imagine themselves in it. Using wealth to win respect often fails — humility, kindness and empathy earn more respect than possessions.
keyIdeas: People don't admire you for your car.
chapters.tryThis: Before a status purchase, ask who you're trying to impress.

quiz.question: What do people think when they see a fancy car?
quiz.explanation: Admiration goes to the car, not the driver.

chapters.title: Wealth is What You Don't See
chapters.summary: Spending is visible; wealth is the money you didn't spend. It's easy to mistake high spenders for rich people. True wealth is unspent assets — options and flexibility waiting to be used.
chapters.tryThis: Track your net worth, not your spending, this month.

quiz.question: What is wealth according to Housel?
quiz.explanation: Wealth is hidden in what you keep.

chapters.title: Save Money
chapters.summary: Your savings rate is more within your control than your returns or income. You don't need a specific reason to save; savings give flexibility for the unknown. Lowering your ego and wants raises savings fastest.
chapters.tryThis: Raise your savings rate by 1% this month.

quiz.question: Do you need a specific reason to save per Housel?
options: No — savings give flexibility for the unknown
quiz.explanation: Savings are a hedge against surprises.

chapters.title: Reasonable > Rational
chapters.summary: Aiming to be mathematically optimal can backfire if you can't stick with the plan. A reasonable strategy you can live with — and won't abandon in a downturn — often beats a 'rational' one you'll quit.
chapters.tryThis: Choose an investment plan you'd keep even after a 30% drop.

quiz.question: Why prefer reasonable over rational?
options: You're more likely to stick with it
quiz.explanation: A plan you keep beats a plan you abandon.

chapters.title: Surprise!
chapters.summary: History is a study of surprises. The biggest economic events were unprecedented, so relying on history to predict the future is risky. Use history to understand behaviour, not to forecast specific events.
chapters.tryThis: Write how your plans would cope with an event no one expects.

quiz.question: How should history be used per Housel?
quiz.explanation: Patterns of behaviour repeat; events don't.

chapters.title: Room for Error
chapters.summary: Leave a margin of safety in everything — savings, debt, timelines — because the future is uncertain. Room for error lets you endure a range of outcomes and stay in the game long enough to benefit from compounding.
chapters.tryThis: Add a buffer to one budget or deadline.

quiz.question: What does 'room for error' allow?
quiz.explanation: Buffers keep you in the game.

chapters.title: You'll Change
chapters.summary: People underestimate how much their goals and desires will change (the 'end of history illusion'). Avoid extreme financial plans, accept that you'll change your mind, and be willing to move on from old decisions without regret.
keyIdeas: Your future self will want different things.
chapters.tryThis: Review a long-term plan and ask if it still fits you.

quiz.question: What is the 'end of history illusion'?
quiz.explanation: We think we've stopped changing — we haven't.

chapters.title: Nothing's Free
chapters.summary: Market volatility is the price of admission for long-term returns, not a fine for doing something wrong. Accepting that fee — fear, uncertainty, drawdowns — makes it easier to stay invested.
keyIdeas: Volatility is a fee, not a fine.
chapters.tryThis: Write down the drop you're willing to accept as the 'fee' for returns.

quiz.question: How does Housel frame volatility?

chapters.title: You & Me
chapters.summary: Investors play different games with different time horizons. Bubbles form when short-term traders set prices that long-term investors mistakenly follow. Know which game you're playing and don't take cues from people playing another.
chapters.tryThis: Write your investing time horizon and goal.

quiz.question: Why do bubbles form per Housel?
options: Long-term investors follow short-term traders' prices

chapters.title: The Seduction of Pessimism
chapters.summary: Pessimism sounds smarter and gets more attention than optimism, yet progress usually happens slowly and quietly while setbacks are sudden. Be a 'reasonable optimist' who expects setbacks but believes in long-term progress.
keyIdeas: Progress is slow; setbacks are fast.
chapters.tryThis: Balance one negative headline with a long-term trend you can check.

quiz.question: Why does pessimism seem smarter?
options: It sounds more credible and urgent

chapters.title: When You'll Believe Anything
chapters.summary: When we want something to be true, we fill gaps in our knowledge with appealing stories. Incentives and desire shape belief, so be most careful with stories that tell you what you want to hear.
chapters.tryThis: Find the strongest argument against an investment you like.

quiz.question: When are we most likely to believe a story?
options: When we want it to be true

chapters.title: All Together Now
chapters.summary: Housel summarises: stay humble when things go well and forgiving when they go wrong, manage risk, save, plan for room for error, favour long time horizons, accept volatility and define the game you're playing.
keyIdeas: Save and leave room for error.
chapters.tryThis: Pick the one lesson from this book you'll apply this month.

quiz.question: Which is part of Housel's summary?
options: Save and leave room for error

chapters.title: Confessions
chapters.summary: Housel shares his own approach: aiming for independence over luxury, saving heavily, avoiding debt on his home, holding cash, and investing simply in low-cost index funds for decades — choices that are reasonable for him rather than optimal for everyone.
chapters.tryThis: Write a one-paragraph money philosophy of your own.

quiz.question: What does Housel prioritise personally?
